title: Parallel Stages
statement: A workshop has tasks numbered 0 to tasks - 1. Each prerequisite [a, b] means task a must be finished before task b can start. Work happens in stages: in one stage you may run any number of tasks at the same time, but a task may only run in a stage if all of its prerequisites were finished in earlier stages. Return the smallest number of stages needed to finish every task, or -1 if the prerequisites contain a cycle, so some task can never run.
constraints: Each prerequisite is [a, b] with 0 <= a, b < tasks and a != b; the same pair may appear more than once

examples.explanation: Stage 1 runs task 0, stage 2 runs tasks 1 and 2 together, stage 3 runs task 3 and stage 4 runs task 4.
Every task waits for another, so none can ever start.

hints.content: Draw the tasks as a graph with an arrow from each prerequisite to the task it unlocks.
A task can run in the first stage exactly when it has no prerequisites. Running them frees up the tasks that were only waiting for them.
Count, for every task, how many prerequisites are still unfinished. Tasks whose count is zero form the next stage.
Process stage by stage: collect all tasks whose count is zero, count one stage, and decrement the counts of everything they unlock; newly zeroed tasks form the next stage.
If the stages finish but fewer than all tasks were run, the remaining tasks wait on each other in a cycle, so return -1.

testCases.explanation: A diamond followed by one more task takes four stages.
A chain forces one task per stage.
Duplicate prerequisites do not add stages.
A cycle in one corner makes the whole plan impossible even though other tasks can finish.
Task 5 waits on both the short and the long route, so the long route sets its stage.
A layered plan with 60 layers of 40 tasks: the number of stages equals the number of layers.

solutions.title: Simulate each stage by rescanning everything
solutions.intuition: Run the plan literally: in each stage find every unfinished task whose prerequisites are all done.
solutions.approach: Repeat: mark every task that still has an unfinished prerequisite as blocked by scanning all prerequisites, run every unfinished unblocked task as one stage, and stop with -1 if no task could run.
solutions.pseudocode:
done = set(); stages = 0
while |done| < tasks:
  blocked = {b for (a, b) in prereqs if a not in done}
  batch = tasks not in done and not in blocked
  if batch is empty: return -1
  done += batch; stages += 1
return stages
solutions.timeComplexity: O(stages * (tasks + prerequisites)), which is O(tasks * (tasks + prerequisites)) in the worst case
commonMistakes: Letting a task run in the same stage as its prerequisite.
Looping forever when a cycle leaves no runnable task.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This simulates the statement and is easy to trust: each pass computes who is unblocked, runs them, and repeats. Rescanning every prerequisite on every stage makes it quadratic on long chains, because a chain of n tasks needs n stages of O(n) work. Counting unfinished prerequisites per task removes the rescans.

steps.title: Stage 1
steps.content: Only task 0 is unblocked in the first example.

steps.title: Later stages
steps.content: Then {1, 2}, {3} and {4} become unblocked, giving four stages. On a cycle no task is unblocked, so -1 is returned.

solutions.title: Level-by-level topological sort
solutions.intuition: Tasks whose unfinished-prerequisite count is zero are exactly the next stage. Finishing them lowers other tasks' counts.
solutions.approach: Build unlock lists and prerequisite counts. Start with all tasks of count zero. Per stage, count it, finish the ready tasks and decrement the counts of the tasks they unlock; those that reach zero form the next stage. If fewer than all tasks were finished, there is a cycle.
solutions.pseudocode:
waiting[b] += 1 and unlocks[a].push(b) for each (a, b)
ready = tasks with waiting == 0; stages = 0; finished = 0
while ready: stages += 1; finished += |ready|
  next = []
  for t in ready: for b in unlocks[t]: waiting[b] -= 1; if 0: next.push(b)
  ready = next
return stages if finished == tasks else -1
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(tasks + prerequisites) for the unlock lists, counts and ready lists
commonMistakes: Counting one stage per task instead of per batch of ready tasks.
Returning the number of stages without checking that every task finished, which hides a cycle.
Mixing up the edge direction, so a task unlocks its own prerequisites.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is Kahn's algorithm run one level at a time. Each level is the set of tasks whose prerequisites all finished earlier, so the number of levels equals the length of the longest prerequisite chain, which is the minimum number of stages. Every task and every prerequisite is touched once, so it is O(tasks + prerequisites) time and space. If a cycle exists its tasks never reach count zero, the finished count stays below the total, and the answer is -1.

steps.title: Count prerequisites
steps.content: In the first example the counts are task 0: 0, tasks 1 and 2: 1, task 3: 2, task 4: 1.

steps.title: Run the levels
steps.content: Level 1 = {0}; it zeroes tasks 1 and 2. Level 2 = {1, 2}; it zeroes task 3. Level 3 = {3}; level 4 = {4}.

steps.title: Check completion
steps.content: All five tasks finished in four stages, so the answer is 4.
